Chapter 6. The Role of Philosophy—Clarifying Thought, Not Explaining the World.
Now that we've explored the boundaries of language and meaning, let's pause and really think about what philosophy is all about.
Instead of chasing after grand theories or digging for hidden truths about how the world works, maybe philosophy's real purpose is something much simpler, and honestly, more helpful. What if its main job is to help us get clear on how we actually use language, and to gently untangle the knots we tie ourselves into when we push language too far?
In this way, philosophy isn’t an all-knowing sage handing out answers—it’s more like a wise, patient guide, quietly showing us where our words just can’t go any further. Think about those moments when we try to talk about things that can’t really be pictured or put into words, like the ultimate nature of reality, or what the self truly is.
We usually end up confused, right? The philosopher’s role here isn’t to solve these mysteries, but to help us see why the questions themselves can’t be answered in the way we expect.
Here are a few key points to keep in mind.
First, philosophy’s main role is to clarify how we use language.
Second, a lot of philosophical problems actually come from misunderstandings about where language runs out of steam.
Third, philosophers help us notice exactly where language just stops working in a meaningful way.
And finally, the biggest insights often come not by saying more, but by realizing what simply can’t be said.
Here’s an image that might help: picture a tangled ball of string. Philosophy doesn’t add more string to the mess or invent new types of knots. Instead, it patiently works to untangle what’s already there, slowly revealing a hidden, simple order underneath. In practice, this means looking closely at how we use words, spotting where confusion creeps in, and learning to set aside questions that can’t really be answered within the rules of language.
This approach naturally brings a sense of humility. It teaches us to value clarity, precision, and honesty in our thinking, instead of chasing after answers that always seem just out of reach. In that way, philosophy becomes a kind of therapy for the mind—helping us find peace by accepting the limits of what can be known, and what can be said.
